teaser: A father's two hands on a ragged back: the quietest reunion in painting.
review_notes:
Date: usually given as about 1668 to 1669; catalog year 1669 kept.
Size 262 x 205 cm.
Identification of the standing man at right as the elder brother is the common reading, not certain; some scholars think the background figures were finished by another hand.
Observation that the father's two hands differ (one broader, one more slender) comes largely from Henri Nouwen's 1992 book; it is an interpretation.
Kenneth Clark's praise is paraphrased, not quoted.
Catherine the Great's purchase dated 1766.
Titus died 1668 aged 26; Hendrickje died 1663; Rembrandt buried in an unmarked rented grave in the Westerkerk, October 1669.
Nouwen first saw a poster of the painting in 1983 and visited the Hermitage in 1986.

lesson.text: Has anyone ever forgiven you before you had finished apologizing? Keep that feeling in mind. It is the whole subject of this painting, which is 2.6 meters tall (about 8 ft 7 in), so the figures are roughly the size of real people.

The story is a parable, a short teaching tale told by Jesus. A younger son demands his inheritance early, leaves home and wastes all of it. Starving, reduced to feeding pigs, he walks back to ask for a servant's job. His father sees him coming and runs out to hold him before he can get the words out.

Rembrandt does not paint the running or the feast that follows. He stops at the embrace, and he tells you what the son has been through without showing his face. The evidence is all on his back, his head and his feet.

lesson.title: The road home
lesson.text: Read the kneeling figure from the ground up.

spots.title: The bare foot
spots.text: The left sandal has fallen off. The sole is scarred and filthy, the foot of someone who has walked a very long way.

spots.title: The broken shoe
spots.text: The other shoe is still on, barely. Its heel is worn through and the sole has collapsed. This is all that is left of the inheritance.

spots.title: The tunic
spots.text: His yellowish tunic is patched and torn and tied with a cord. Rembrandt paints the rags in thick, crusted strokes.

spots.title: The shaved head
spots.text: His hair is cropped to the skull like a prisoner's or a newborn's. He presses his face sideways into his father's chest, eyes closed.

lesson.text: He has lost his money, his hair, his shoes. Yet Rembrandt leaves him one object from his old life. It is small and dark, and most visitors walk past it.
The son still carries one thing that marks him as a gentleman's child. It hangs at his hip. Can you find it?

spots.title: The short sword
spots.text: A small dagger in its sheath hangs from his belt. He sold or lost everything else, but he kept the sign of the family he came from. Part of him never stopped being a son.

lesson.text: Now the father. His face is tilted down, and his eyes seem almost closed, as if he were recognizing his child by touch. Everything he has to say is in his hands, spread flat on the boy's shoulders. They sit at the brightest point of the canvas.

Many viewers find that the two hands do not match. The one on the left looks broad and strong and grips the shoulder. The one on the right is narrower and rests more lightly. Some read them as a father's hand and a mother's hand.

When he painted this, in the last year or two of his life, Rembrandt knew loss from the father's side. His partner Hendrickje had died in 1663. In 1668 his only surviving son, Titus, died at 26. Rembrandt followed in October 1669 and was buried in an unmarked grave.

About thirty years earlier, Rembrandt had painted the same parable from the other end. In that picture, a laughing young man raises a tall glass in a tavern with a woman on his knee. It is usually read as the prodigal son wasting his money, with Rembrandt himself as the model.
The embrace takes up only the left side. The rest of the huge canvas belongs to people who watch and do nothing. Their silence is part of the story.

spots.title: The standing man
spots.text: He is tall and bearded and wears the same red as the father. Most viewers take him for the elder brother, the dutiful one who stayed home. His face is lit but shows nothing.

spots.title: Clasped hands
spots.text: Compare these with the father's. His are open and laid on his son. These are locked together around a staff and kept to himself.

spots.title: The seated man
spots.text: He wears a black beret and a mustache, and one arm rests across his chest. He leans in and watches closely but does not move from his seat.

spots.title: The woman in the dark
spots.text: A face floats in the shadows behind the group, barely more than a sketch. No one knows who she is meant to be.

spots.title: The father's face
spots.text: He is old and bearded, with heavy lowered eyelids. The red cloak opens over the boy like a roof.

lesson.text: The parable ends with the elder brother refusing to join the party, angry that the wasteful one gets a welcome. Rembrandt folds that ending into the same room. Forgiveness is being given on the left and judged on the right, and there is a wide dark gap between them.
Empress Catherine the Great of Russia bought the painting in 1766 for her new collection in Saint Petersburg. It has been one of the treasures of the Hermitage ever since.
Rembrandt reduced a whole story to a gesture. The son does not show his face and nobody speaks, and two hands on a back are enough to say “you are home.”

In 1983 a Dutch priest named Henri Nouwen saw a poster of this picture pinned to a door, and it stayed with him. He later traveled to the Hermitage and sat in front of it for days. His book about it is still read around the world. He started out seeing himself in the kneeling son, then recognized himself in the brother, and in the end he felt the painting was asking him to become the father.

quiz.question: What is a parable?
quiz.explanation: The prodigal son is a teaching tale told by Jesus.

quiz.question: Which object shows that the son still belongs to a good family?
options: A small dagger at his hip
quiz.explanation: He kept his short sword when everything else was gone.

quiz.question: How does the lesson describe the father's two hands?
options: They are hidden in his cloak
They are raised in blessing above the son
They look different from one another
quiz.explanation: One seems broad and strong, the other narrower and lighter.

quiz.question: What had happened to Rembrandt shortly before he painted this?
quiz.explanation: Titus died in 1668 at the age of 26.

quiz.question: Who brought the painting to Saint Petersburg?

facts.text: The son's face is turned toward us, in tears.
facts.explanation: He is seen from behind, his face pressed into his father's chest.

facts.text: One of the son's feet is bare.
facts.explanation: His left sandal has fallen off, showing a scarred sole.

facts.text: Rembrandt painted this picture as a young man in his twenties.
facts.explanation: It dates from the last year or two of his life.
